section.title: Functions as assignments
section.p: The real line gave us a language for position, distance, intervals, and error. Calculus begins when one number on that line determines another.
A time determines a position. A radius determines an area. A temperature determines the volume of a gas. A step size h determines the error in an approximation.
That kind of dependence is called a function.

subsection.title: Input, output, domain, and range
subsection.p: Imagine a trip along a straight road. At each time t, the car has a position s(t). The input is time. The output is position:
For example, if the car moves at 50 miles/hour starting from position 0, then
This formula assigns one position to each time:

figure.caption: A function assigns an output to each input in its domain.

subsection.p: The word assigns is important. A function is not merely a formula. It is a rule that gives exactly one output for each allowed input.

statement.p: A function f from a set D to the real numbers is a rule that assigns to each input x\in D exactly one real number f(x).
The set D is called the domain of f.
The set of all outputs is called the range of f:

subsection.p: We often write f:D\to \mathbb{R}. This means that the inputs come from D, and the outputs are real numbers.

statement.p: Let f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}, f(x)=x^2.
The domain is all real numbers. The range is [0,\infty), because every square is nonnegative, and every nonnegative number is the square of some real number.
For instance, 9 is in the range because f(3)=9. But -4 is not in the range because no real number has square -4.

A function is a rule together with its allowed inputs.

subsection.title: Functions from formulas, graphs, tables, and words
subsection.p: A formula is the most familiar way to describe a function, but it is not the only way.

paragraphs.title: A function from a formula
paragraphs.p: The area A of a circle depends on its radius r:
If the radius is measured in centimeters, then the area is measured in square centimeters. The natural domain is [0,\infty), because a radius cannot be negative.

paragraphs.title: A function from a table
paragraphs.p: A thermometer may record the temperature of a cup of tea every minute:
This table defines a function on the domain \{0,1,2,3,4\}. For example, T(2)=75.
The table does not tell us the exact temperature at t=2.5. It may suggest one, but it does not assign one unless we add more information.
This distinction will matter later. Data can suggest a model, but the model is a new function.

paragraphs.title: A function from a graph
paragraphs.p: A graph can also describe a function. The input x is read along the horizontal axis. The output f(x) is read along the vertical axis.

A graph represents a function only when each input gives exactly one output. This is the reason for the vertical line test: a vertical line corresponds to one input x. If it hits a curve in two places, then that input has two possible outputs, so the curve is not the graph of a function of x.

figure.caption: The full circle gives two y-values for many x-values. The upper semicircle gives exactly one.

paragraphs.p: The circle x^2+y^2=1 is not the graph of y as a function of x, because most inputs x between -1 and 1 give two outputs.
But the upper semicircle y=\sqrt{1-x^2} is a function on the domain [-1,1].

paragraphs.title: A function from words
paragraphs.p: Sometimes the rule is best described in words. For example:
paragraphs.md: C(m)=\text{the cost, in dollars, of a taxi ride of }m\text{ miles}.
paragraphs.p: Here 4 is the starting charge, and 2.50 is the cost per mile. The units help us read the formula:
The natural domain is [0,\infty), or perhaps a smaller interval if the taxi company serves only local trips.

remark.p: When you meet a function, ask four questions:

subsection.title: The natural domain of a formula
subsection.p: When a formula is given without an explicit domain, we usually take the domain to be all real numbers for which the formula makes sense. This is called the natural domain.

statement.p: For f(x)=\frac{1}{x-2}, the denominator cannot be 0. Therefore x\neq 2.
The natural domain is (-\infty,2)\cup(2,\infty).
For g(x)=\sqrt{x-1}, the quantity under the square root must be nonnegative: x-1\ge 0.
So x\ge 1, and the natural domain is [1,\infty).
For h(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}, we need 4-x^2\ge 0.
This means x^2\le 4, so -2\le x\le 2. The natural domain is [-2,2].
In fact, the graph of y=\sqrt{4-x^2} is the upper half of the circle x^2+y^2=4. The domain is the horizontal interval covered by the semicircle. The range is [0,2].

subsection.title: Piecewise-defined functions
subsection.p: Many real processes follow one rule for a while and then another rule later.

A car may move forward, stop at a light, then reverse into a parking space. A tax bill may use one rate for the first part of income and another rate for the next part. A postage cost may stay constant over a range of weights, then jump.
These functions are often described piece by piece.

statement.p: A car starts at position 0, moves forward at 40 miles/hour for 2 hours, and then moves backward at 30 miles/hour for 1 hour.
For 0\le t\le 2, the position is s(t)=40t.
At t=2, the car has reached s(2)=80.
After that, the car moves backward at 30 miles/hour. For 2\lt t\le 3, its position is
Thus
The domain is [0,3]. The range is [0,80], because the car starts at 0, reaches 80, and then returns to 50.

figure.caption: A piecewise function can describe motion whose rule changes.

subsection.p: At t=2, the definition uses only the first formula. That is enough. A function must give one output for each input, not two.
Here the second formula would also give 80-30(2-2)=80, so there would be no conflict if we included t=2 in both pieces. But it is cleaner to assign the boundary point once.

remark.title: Why this matters
remark.p: The derivative will come from the difference quotient by letting h move toward 0. Before taking that limit, we need to know where the quotient is defined.

subsection.p: Functions let one quantity depend on another. Graphs let us see that dependence all at once. Before we can study limits on graphs, we need to learn how graphs move, stretch, reflect, and reveal information.
